doc.title: Joseph Rene and Edna Kelly Interview, 1969-12-15

chapter: Joe Rene: Lewis, the Rena band and New Orleans
title: Chris Kelly, Kid Rena's tone, and tailgate wagon battles
summary: Rene calls Chris Kelly a country blues player, praises his brother's tone, and describes tailgate wagon contests between bands.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Chris Kelly, the blues trumpeter and his band

blocks.x: No, he started out there in the country down the, like the fella said, down the bayou, yeah. So, he was mostly of a blues player. He was, he was, like this, what you call it, I would call it at that time, not a, a blues player, that's all we would say. Yes, yes. He could play blues, you know, he could play that. He played other things, but he wouldn't have had a nice tone in his trumpet. My brother had the best tone in the world. Yeah. According to what this, uh, this, uh, French professor in France said, you know. Oh, yeah. And, they, they went and viewed him some of them, and, and he was talking about the colored trumpet players. And, they, they all of them. And, they said, my brother had the best tone, the best tone trumpet. Oh, yeah.

Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. And, you see, his jaws was flattened. You see no jaws popping like that. Played this as smooth. He wasn't excited about nothing. Mm-hmm. At that time, we had, they used to call, you ever heard of him talking about the tailgate? We used to be advertising, and, well, at one place we started in the furniture way. Two mules. Then, after that, there came, uh, these trucks. And, the trombone player, and the bass player, the one, beat all the tailgates. All the rest of the music. Yeah. Yeah. There used to be a time, man. We used to meet them bands, meet on the corner, man. And, they tied them trucks together. All the people, you know, people outside did that. They know he's gonna beat them bands.
